text: With George Willard beside him. <break time="0.8s" /> Wing lost some of his timidity. <break time="0.8s" /> And the shadowy self. <break time="0.8s" /> Usually buried under his doubts. <break time="0.8s" /> Came out to look at the world. <break time="0.8s" /> When he talked with the young reporter. <break time="0.8s" /> His voice, which had been low and trembling. <break time="0.8s" /> Became loud and sharp. <break time="0.8s" /> And his bent body straightened. <break time="0.8s" /> Then his slender, expressive fingers. <break time="0.8s" /> Would begin to beat upon a table. <break time="0.8s" /> Or the top board of a fence. <break time="0.8s" /> And this seemed to make him more comfortable. <break time="0.8s" /> The story of Wing Biddlebaum. <break time="0.8s" /> Is a story of hands. <break time="0.8s" /> And their restless activity. <break time="0.8s" /> Like the beating wings of a caged bird. <break time="0.8s" /> Had given him his name. <break time="0.8s" /> Wing tried to keep his hands hidden. <break time="0.8s" /> And he looked with wonder. <break time="0.8s" /> At the quiet hands of other men. <break time="0.8s" /> Who worked beside him in the fields. <break time="0.8s" /> In Winesburg the hands. <break time="0.8s" /> Had attracted attention. <break time="0.8s" /> Merely because of their activity. <break time="0.8s" /> And with them he had once picked. <break time="0.8s" /> As many as a hundred and forty quarts. <break time="0.8s" /> Of strawberries in a day. <break time="0.8s" /> The town was proud of his hands. <break time="0.8s" /> In the same way that it was proud of Banker Whites new stone house. <break time="0.8s" /> And Wesley Moyers trotting stallion, Tony Tip. <break time="0.8s" /> Although George Willard had often felt. <break time="0.8s" /> A strong curiosity about the hands. <break time="0.8s" /> Only his growing respect for the old man. <break time="0.8s" /> Had kept him from asking.
